newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. refugee chief seeks Zaire solution.
newsitem.headline: U.N. refugee chief seeks Zaire solution.

text.p: U.N. refugee agency chief Sadako Ogata called for a political and security solution to the crisis in east Zaire before leaving for the region where UNHCR says 40,000 refugees are on the run.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees told Reuters that an international force could have solved much of the problems in the region, where rebels are fighting Zairean forces and Rwandan Hutu refugees are fleeing.
"Political and security solutions are paramount. What the humanitarian community can say is to show the great suffering people are exposed to without a political solution," she said.

Ogata, who has criticised the West's desire for "quick-fix" solutions to Africa's worst refugee crisis instead of sending in troops to separate Hutu militiamen from refugees, said an international force was needed.

"If an international force had been deployed the way they had originally been foreseen, I think a lot of the problems we're struggling with might have been prevented or might have been contained," she said.
Western countries led by the United States abandoned the idea of the force after more than half of 1.1 million Hutu refugees in Zaire returned home after rebel victories in 1996.

But UNHCR says up to 400,000 remain in the region, where unconfirmed reports say rebels are pushing towards the Lubutu area, 240 km (150 miles) southeast of regional capital Kisangani and shelter to 200,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Ogata said 40,000 refugees had left Shabunda, which the rebels said they captured on Wednesday.
She said a UNHCR plane would fly over the area on Friday to try to find the refugees in the middle of the thick rain forest.
Ogata meets Zairean leaders on Friday in capital Kinshasa and will then fly down to the refugee area. "I will go as far as I can go," she said.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has said he is ready to open corridors for the refugees and he urged the UNHCR to approach him to work out arrangements.
Ogata ruled out direct talks with Kabila and the rebels although she said any talks to open humanitarian corridors would have to involve groups in control on the ground.
Ogata will also visit Rwanda, where gunmen killed five U.N. human rights staff on Tuesday, as well as Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda.
She condemned the killings in Rwanda but said the NHCR would not pull out of the country, where more than half a million minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates died in 1994's Hutu-led genocide.
"It is a very worrying situation that is developing. Humanitarian staff are really at the forefront of today's conflicts. I condemn these things in the strongest terms," she said.
"But in Rwanda, we have returnees...It is not an area we can leave easily. The government is promising better security situation and we'll try to continue our operation."
